prompt: How are alcohols classified as primary (1°), secondary (2°), or tertiary (3°)?

choices.text: By the number of organic groups on the hydroxyl-bearing carbon
By the number of –OH groups the molecule contains
choices.why: A molecule with two –OH groups is a diol, whatever its class. The 1°/2°/3° label looks only at the hydroxyl-bearing carbon.

choices.text: By the number of carbons in the longest chain holding the –OH
choices.why: Chain length sets the parent name, not the class. Only the groups on the hydroxyl-bearing carbon count.

choices.text: By the number of hydrogens bonded to the oxygen atom
choices.why: Every alcohol has just one hydrogen on its oxygen. The classification looks at the carbon that carries the –OH.

explanation: Alcohols are classified as primary (1°), secondary (2°), or tertiary (3°) depending on the number of organic groups bonded to the hydroxyl-bearing carbon: one R group for primary, two for secondary, three for tertiary.

prompt: Is 2-methyl-1-propanol, (CH3)2CHCH2OH, a primary, secondary, or tertiary alcohol?

choices.why: The –OH is on a CH2 carbon bonded to only one organic group, (CH3)2CH–. The branch is one carbon farther away and doesn't count.
A tertiary alcohol has three organic groups on the hydroxyl-bearing carbon. Here that carbon is a CH2 with just one.

choices.text: It can't be classified, because the chain is branched
choices.why: Branching elsewhere in the chain doesn't matter. Only the groups on the hydroxyl-bearing carbon decide the class.

explanation: Look only at the carbon that carries the –OH. In (CH3)2CHCH2OH it is a CH2 bonded to one organic group, the (CH3)2CH– group, so the alcohol is primary even though the chain is branched.

prompt: How many of these five alcohols are secondary: 1-butanol, 2-butanol, 2-methyl-2-propanol, cyclohexanol, and 2-methyl-1-propanol?
explanation: 2-Butanol, CH3CH(OH)CH2CH3, and cyclohexanol each have two organic groups on the hydroxyl-bearing carbon, so they are secondary. 1-Butanol and 2-methyl-1-propanol are primary (one group), and 2-methyl-2-propanol, (CH3)3COH, is tertiary (three groups).

prompt: Why is CH3CH2CH2OH named propanol rather than propaneol?

choices.text: The -e of the alkane name is deleted so that two vowels don't sit next to each other
The -e is deleted in every alcohol name, whatever letter follows it
choices.why: The -e stays when the next letter is a consonant, as in cyclohexanediol.

choices.text: Propane loses a hydrogen atom when the –OH is attached, so its name is shortened
choices.why: The rule is about spelling, not atoms: the -e is deleted to avoid two adjacent vowels.

choices.text: Propaneol is reserved for the alcohol with the –OH on carbon 2
choices.why: Propaneol isn't used for any alcohol. The position of the –OH is shown by a locant, as in 2-propanol.

explanation: Rule 1: the parent name comes from the alkane by replacing its -e ending with -ol. The -e is deleted to prevent two adjacent vowels: propanol rather than propaneol.

prompt: Why is cis-1,4-cyclohexanediol not spelled cis-1,4-cyclohexandiol?

choices.text: The -e stays because the next letter, d, is not a vowel
The -e is always kept in the names of cyclic alcohols
choices.why: Cyclohexanol drops the -e because the next letter, o, is a vowel. Being cyclic has nothing to do with it.

choices.text: The -e shows that the ring contains a double bond
choices.why: Cyclohexanediol has no double bond. The -diol suffix means two –OH groups.

choices.text: The cis prefix requires the full alkane name to be kept
choices.why: cis only tells you that the two –OH groups are on the same face of the ring. It doesn't affect the spelling.

explanation: The -e of the alkane name is deleted only to prevent two adjacent vowels. In cyclohexanediol the suffix begins with d, a consonant, so the -e stays: cyclohexanediol rather than cyclohexandiol.

prompt: What is the IUPAC name of CH3CH2CH(CH3)CH2CH(OH)CH3?

choices.why: This numbers the chain from the wrong end. Rule 2 says to start at the end nearer the hydroxyl group, which puts the –OH on carbon 2.
The parent must be the longest chain containing the –OH. Running through the ethyl group gives six carbons, so the parent is hexanol.
Count again: the longest chain containing the –OH has six carbons, not five.

explanation: The longest chain containing the –OH has six carbons (hexanol). Numbering from the end nearer the –OH puts it on carbon 2 and the methyl group on carbon 4: 4-methyl-2-hexanol (4-methylhexan-2-ol in the newer style).

prompt: Newer IUPAC recommendations place the locant immediately before the suffix. What is the newer name for 3-phenyl-2-butanol?

choices.why: The numbering doesn't change with the naming style. The –OH still gets the lower number, carbon 2.
That is the older name, with the locant in front of the parent.
Only the final -e of butane is dropped before -ol, so the parent stays butan-: butan-2-ol.

explanation: In the newer style the locant goes right before the suffix: 3-phenyl-2-butanol becomes 3-phenylbutan-2-ol, just as 2-methyl-2-pentanol becomes 2-methylpentan-2-ol and cis-1,4-cyclohexanediol becomes cis-cyclohexane-1,4-diol.

prompt: What is the IUPAC name of C6H5CH2CH2C(OH)(CH3)2?

choices.why: This numbers from the wrong end. The chain is numbered from the end nearer the –OH, which puts it on carbon 2.
The parent must be the longest chain containing the –OH. Including one of the methyl groups gives a four-carbon chain, butanol.
Substituents are listed in alphabetical order, so methyl comes before phenyl.

explanation: The longest chain containing the –OH has four carbons (butanol). Numbering from the end nearer the –OH puts the –OH and one methyl on carbon 2 and the phenyl on carbon 4. Listing substituents alphabetically gives 2-methyl-4-phenyl-2-butanol (Exercise 17.1.1).

prompt: What is the IUPAC name of CH3CH(OH)CH2CH(OH)CH(CH3)2?

choices.why: Numbering starts from the end nearer the hydroxyl groups. That gives them locants 2 and 4, lower than 3 and 5.
The -e of hexane is kept, because the suffix -diol begins with d, a consonant.
The longest chain has six carbons. The methyl on carbon 5 is a branch, not part of the chain.

explanation: The longest chain has six carbons and two –OH groups (a hexanediol, keeping the -e). Numbering from the end nearer the –OH groups puts them on carbons 2 and 4 and the methyl on carbon 5: 5-methyl-2,4-hexanediol (Exercise 17.1.1).

prompt: A cyclopentane ring has an –OH group on one carbon and a bromine on the next carbon, with the –OH and the –Br on opposite faces of the ring. What is its name?

choices.why: cis means both groups are on the same face of the ring. Here they are on opposite faces, so the compound is trans.
The hydroxyl-bearing carbon is carbon 1, so the bromine is on carbon 2.
The ring has five carbons, so the parent is cyclopentanol.

explanation: The parent is cyclopentanol, and the hydroxyl-bearing carbon is numbered 1, so the bromine is on carbon 2. Groups on opposite faces of a ring are trans: trans-2-bromocyclopentanol (Exercise 17.1.1).

prompt: A benzene ring carries an –OH group, a methyl group meta to the –OH, and a bromine para to the –OH (so the methyl and bromine are on neighboring carbons). What is the compound's name?

choices.why: Substituents are listed in alphabetical order, so bromo comes before methyl.
Number around the ring in the direction that gives the lower locants: 3 and 4, not 4 and 5.
Phenols are named with -phenol as the parent name rather than -benzene.

explanation: Phenols are named like other aromatic compounds, with -phenol as the parent and the hydroxyl-bearing carbon as carbon 1. Numbering toward the methyl puts it on carbon 3 and the bromine on carbon 4, and the substituents are listed alphabetically: 4-bromo-3-methylphenol (Exercise 17.1.1).

prompt: A cyclopentene ring has an –OH group on a carbon right next to one of the double-bond carbons. What is its name?

choices.why: The hydroxyl-bearing carbon gets number 1, so the double bond begins at carbon 2.
In 3-cyclopenten-1-ol the double bond starts at carbon 3, so it isn't next to the hydroxyl-bearing carbon.
That name would put the –OH on one of the double-bond carbons, not next to them.

explanation: The –OH carbon is numbered 1, and numbering continues toward the double bond, which then begins at carbon 2: 2-cyclopenten-1-ol (Exercise 17.1.1).

prompt: Which IUPAC-accepted common name belongs to 1,2,3-propanetriol?

choices.why: Ethylene glycol is 1,2-ethanediol, with two carbons and two –OH groups.
Allyl alcohol is 2-propen-1-ol, with one –OH group and a double bond.
tert-Butyl alcohol is 2-methyl-2-propanol, with a single –OH group.

explanation: Some simple alcohols have common names accepted by IUPAC: benzyl alcohol (phenylmethanol), allyl alcohol (2-propen-1-ol), tert-butyl alcohol (2-methyl-2-propanol), ethylene glycol (1,2-ethanediol), and glycerol (1,2,3-propanetriol), which has an –OH on each of its three carbons.

prompt: In 2,4-dinitrophenol, where are the two nitro groups relative to the –OH group?

choices.why: That would be 2,6-dinitrophenol. Carbon 4 is across the ring from carbon 1, the para position.
A meta nitro group would be on carbon 3 or 5. Carbon 4 is para.
That would be 3,5-dinitrophenol.

explanation: In a phenol name the hydroxyl-bearing carbon is carbon 1. Carbon 2 is next to it (ortho) and carbon 4 is directly across the ring (para), so 2,4-dinitrophenol has one ortho and one para nitro group.

choices.why: This is 1,5-pentanediol. Its second –OH is on carbon 5, not carbon 4.
This chain has only four carbons, so it is a butanediol.
This is 2,4-pentanediol. Numbered from either end, its –OH groups are on carbons 2 and 4.

explanation: Pentanediol has a five-carbon chain with two –OH groups, and the locants 1 and 4 place them on the first and fourth carbons: HOCH2CH2CH2CH(OH)CH3 (Exercise 17.1.2).
